pillar_reactions.evidence: The standard pillar was never delivered — the rep pivoted to a product demonstration instead — so the reaction is to the platform rather than to the method. He asked the one question that mattered to him: 'within the university, is it like, are they sort of structured workouts as such, or are they just more individual videos of different?' The rep screen-shared the classroom, a six-minute press tutorial, the Primal Mastery twelve-week progressions and the tracking sheet, and the prospect confirmed it answered the question: 'So this is structured workout, yeah? Yeah, yeah. Definitely.' He had already validated the modality on his own body over eight weeks and volunteered the strongest reason it suits him: kettlebells leave him with more energy rather than the concentration crash he gets from endurance work.

Barely presented and needed nothing. The rep covered it in a single sentence inside the platform tour — 'nutrition advice on his idea of eating, which is pretty simple, about what you eat, when you eat, and how much you eat' — and the prospect agreed. Baseline had already established a whole-foods diet he and his wife run deliberately, a past period of veganism abandoned over protein, added whey since restarting, and a two-glasses-of-wine-a-night habit he had dropped eight weeks earlier. The rep validated rather than instructed.

Never delivered, and its absence is the substance of the call rather than an oversight. Accountability is the pillar the $1,000 product strips out, and the rep's disqualification rested precisely on the claim that this prospect does not need it: 'for you it's going to be way easier to pick up on things and like being accountable and being consistent and disciplined, like you already have that.' The prospect had supplied the evidence himself — 'I don't have any issues showing up' and 'I'm not someone that struggles with willpower or motivation.' Worth tracking at renewal: if he lapses when work gets busy in the autumn, exactly as he predicted he might, the pillar he was judged not to need is the one that would have caught it.

anchors.raw: I have found people online with YouTube videos and so on, which are good, but it feels, you know, it's a bit like, Trevor mentions it in some of his videos as well, it can often feel a bit cookie cutter.
anchors.competitor: Free YouTube fitness content generally, including the coach's own
anchors.note: Second consecutive call in this batch where the prospect is already getting results from free content before paying anything — eight weeks of self-directed kettlebell training with visible change. He converted the anchor into a reason to buy on his own ('it just feels a bit random... why am I doing that one?'), which the rep then reinforced well. The recurring shape across this batch is that the free content generates the lead and simultaneously supplies the reason not to purchase.

anchors.raw: financially it's not a hardship, it's just something that I wouldn't want to do without going to speak to her first
anchors.note: Stated twice, unprompted, about a $1,000 product — and this is a man who maintains homes in Andorra and Ibiza and runs his own production company. The strongest affordability signal in the batch relative to the price being asked, and it was collected on a call where the $6,000 option was never mentioned.

anchors.raw: I watch my wife build her kind of yoga routines, you know, for her clients, and I'm like, yeah, I didn't, that's not me, you know, to kind of do the structure of a workout
anchors.competitor: His wife, a practising yoga teacher, and her programme-building
anchors.note: An unusual anchor: the closest available substitute is a qualified coach living in his house, and he used it to argue for buying rather than against. Watching her build client programmes is precisely what convinced him that programming is a skill he does not have. The rep did not notice or use it.

anchors.raw: We'll credit everything that you've already put toward Primal University into the one-on-one coaching program.
anchors.note: A full-value upgrade credit from the $1,000 product into one-to-one coaching, offered verbally and unprompted. Not recorded anywhere else in the corpus; the written agreement read aloud on the Ricky call contains only a $500 renewal credit. It de-risks the downsell and creates a defined upgrade path, and it should either be documented as policy or stopped.

unmet_demand.want: To look inside the platform properly before paying, having been shown a guided tour but no access
unmet_demand.why_unmet: Closed content — 'it's not accessible from people outside.' He accepted it without argument, but it is the reason he asked for the weekend rather than deciding on the call, alongside speaking to his wife. A read-only preview or a short trial would have removed the only stated obstacle to closing on the day.

unmet_demand.want: The option of one-to-one coaching, or at least its price, so he could weigh the choice himself
unmet_demand.why_unmet: Withheld by the rep's judgement rather than by the product. The $6,000 figure was never spoken and the prospect finished the call saying 'I'm looking forward to working with you guys. So in whatever capacity' — which is an open door to the premium tier from an ICP-perfect, financially unconstrained buyer. He cannot want what he was never shown.

unmet_demand.want: Programming that survives travel with no kettlebell access — hotel rooms, location shoots, six months a year in a different country
unmet_demand.why_unmet: Named specifically as the thing that would make the difference in busy periods: 'whether I'm in a hotel room and don't have access to the kettlebells or I have limited time that I can still do it.' The platform includes bodyweight material in its library, but nothing on the call established whether the structured Primal Mastery progressions have equipment-free substitutions, and the self-paced product has no coach to adapt them.
